---
title: "GLORYS Identical-Twin Chain"
jupyter: python3
fig-dpi: 300
bibliography: ../paper/references.bib
---


GLORYS12 is the true ocean: its velocity field moves the virtual floats and its 0--2000 m OHC is the field they
sample. The ocean is held fixed. What is random is where floats are deployed: each replicate redraws the real
2010--2019 launches from a year-stratified smoothed bootstrap and advects them in GLORYS. The target is the annual
mean OHC $\theta_y$ of box A (22--34$^\circ$N, gyre interior), box B (34--45$^\circ$N, Gulf Stream) and A $\cup$ B, for
2015--2019. Bias, variance and MSE are taken over 200 replicates, so they measure how the estimators behave across
deployments of this one ocean. Details are in the theory note (`paper/sections/theory.tex`).

**Estimators**, per replicate and box-year:

* **naive mean**: the average OHC at the in-box float profiles;
* **mean field**: the local-polynomial mean field [@sukianto2026, eq. 5] averaged over the box;
* **map**: the mean field plus locally stationary kriging of its anomalies [@kuusela2018], averaged over the box;
* **DR**: the map plus a $1/\hat q$-weighted mean of its residuals at held-out floats, cross-fitted over $K=5$ float folds.

The map averages over $0.5^\circ$ nodes at three times per month. Checked against the true field, that quadrature
is accurate to 0.01 GJ m$^{-2}$, so all map error below is interpolation error.

# Methods

## Virtual floats

**Deployment pool.** The pool is every real Argo float launched in 2010--2019 inside the GLORYS velocity domain
($11$--$66^\circ$N, $87$--$12^\circ$W) on water at least $1000$ m deep: $994$ floats. Each keeps its launch position
and date (from the GDAC metadata, or its first profile when the metadata are inconsistent) and its operating
life, launch to last profile (median $1380$ d). @fig-deployments shows the launch positions.

::: {#cell-fig-deployments .cell execution_count=2}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![The deployment pool: launch positions of the 994 floats deployed in the velocity domain in 2010-2019, coloured by launch year. Blue dashed: the velocity (advection) domain; green dashed: the OHC field domain; shaded: boxes A and B.](glorys_chain_files/figure-html/fig-deployments-output-1.png){#fig-deployments width=947 height=648}
:::
:::


**Resampling.** A replicate is a year-stratified smoothed bootstrap of the pool. Within each launch year $y$ it
draws the year's $N_y$ floats with replacement, so every replicate has the real yearly counts but a different
set of launches. Each draw is jittered uniformly by $\pm 1/12^\circ$ in latitude and in great-circle longitude
and by $\pm 10$ d in time; a jittered seed off deep water is redrawn. The $265$ floats already profiling on
2010-01-01 enter every replicate unchanged, at their first 2010 position with their remaining life. The random
element of the study is this resampling, one independent draw per replicate.

::: {#cell-fig-deployment-draw .cell execution_count=3}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![One bootstrap draw (replicate 171): the 994 real launch positions (grey, transparent) and the replicate's 994 jittered seeds (solid, coloured by launch year). Sampling with replacement repeats some launches and omits others; this draw uses 651 distinct real launches.](glorys_chain_files/figure-html/fig-deployment-draw-output-1.png){#fig-deployment-draw width=947 height=648}
:::
:::


@fig-deployment-draw shows one draw. Because it samples with replacement, some real launches appear two or more
times and about a third are left out; the jitter is small at this scale, so repeated seeds sit almost on top of each
other.

**Advection.** All floats of a replicate are advected together in one continuous Parcels run through the GLORYS12
daily horizontal velocity at the $1000$ m parking depth, by fourth-order Runge--Kutta with a 1 h step, from
2010-01-01 to the end of 2019. A float is removed when its life runs out or it leaves the domain. Vertical cycling
is not simulated: a profile is taken every $10$ d after release at the float's interpolated parking position. The
years 2010--2014 are a spin-up, so the in-box float population is in equilibrium by the scored years 2015--2019.

::: {#cell-fig-advection .cell execution_count=4}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Replicate 171: 80 randomly chosen deployed floats, their 10-day profile positions and tracks 2010-2019, coloured by profile year. Blue dashed: the velocity (advection) domain; green dashed: the OHC field domain; shaded: boxes A and B.](glorys_chain_files/figure-html/fig-advection-output-1.png){#fig-advection width=947 height=648}
:::
:::


**Profiles.** Each profile reads $Z$ at its containing native cell and day, with no measurement error. The map
uses every profile in the buffer $14$--$55^\circ$N, $72$--$32^\circ$W, from the deployed and the initial floats.
The DR weighting and the folds use only the deployed floats, whose law $\hat q$ describes. There are $1000$
replicates; $\hat q$ uses all of them, and the maps and DR are run on the first $200$. @fig-profile-density shows
where the profiles fall in the scored years: on average $930$ profiles per year in box A and $1170$ in box B per
replicate.

::: {#cell-fig-profile-density .cell execution_count=5}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Deployed-float profiles in 2015-2019 per year and 1 deg cell, mean over the 1000 replicates, relative to the mean over all sampled cells (log scale from 1/4 to 4; red above, blue below the mean), over the velocity domain. Shaded: boxes A and B.](glorys_chain_files/figure-html/fig-profile-density-output-1.png){#fig-profile-density width=947 height=648}
:::
:::


**Quadrature.** The target $\theta_y=\int Z\,d\mathbb P_y$ is an integral; a map is turned into a box-year mean by
the quadrature rule

$$
Q_y(g)=\sum_{m\in y}\frac{d_m}{D_y}\sum_{j}\frac{a_j}{\sum_{j'}a_{j'}}\cdot\frac13\sum_{l=1}^{3}g\bigl(c_j,\;t_m+\tau_l d_m\bigr),
\qquad \tau\in\{\tfrac16,\tfrac12,\tfrac56\}.
$$

Here $m$ runs over the months of year $y$, with $d_m$ days, start $t_m$ and $D_y=\sum_m d_m$; $j$ runs over the
box's $0.5^\circ$ cells, with $a_j$ the area of the cell's water deeper than $2000$ m and $c_j$ its area centroid.
So $Q_y$ is an area-weighted mean over cells at three times per month, and the months are day-weighted. The map and
fold-map estimates are $Q_y(\hat m)$ and $Q_y(\hat m_{-k})$. Applied to the true field, $Q_y(Z)$ differs from
$\theta_y$ by at most $0.01$ GJ m$^{-2}$, so the quadrature remainder $\theta_y-Q_y(Z)$ is negligible next to every
error below.

## Sampling intensity: $q$, $\hat q$ and $w$

Let $\nu$ be area $\times$ time measure on the deep ocean of a box-year $S_y$ and $\mathbb P_y=\nu/\nu(S_y)$ its
normalized version, so $\theta_y=\int Z\,d\mathbb P_y$. One deployment produces a random set of in-box profile
locations $\{s_i\}$, a point process $N$ on $S_y$. Its intensity measure $\Lambda(B)=\mathbb E\,N(B)$, the expected
number of profiles in $B$ over deployments, is absolutely continuous with respect to $\nu$, and

$$
q=\frac{d\Lambda}{d\nu}
$$

is the **sampling intensity**: expected profiles per m$^2$ per day at each place and time. It describes the
deployment law, not one array. A single replicate is one noisy draw from it. Campbell's theorem,
$\mathbb E\sum_i g(s_i)=\int g\,q\,d\nu$, is what makes $1/q$ the right weight. Wherever $q>0$,
$\mathbb E\sum_i g(s_i)/q(s_i)=\int g\,d\nu$, whatever the sampling pattern.

The **normalized intensity** $w=q/\bar q_y$, with $\bar q_y=\int q\,d\mathbb P_y$, is the density of the profile
locations relative to uniform sampling. $w=2$ means twice as many profiles as an even spread would give, and
$w=1/2$ half as many. The naive mean averages $Z$ under $w\,d\mathbb P_y$ instead of $d\mathbb P_y$. Since
$\int w\,d\mathbb P_y=1$,

$$
\int wZ\,d\mathbb P_y-\theta_y=\operatorname{Cov}_{\mathbb P_y}(w,Z),
$$

so floats over-sampling cold water ($w$ and $Z$ negatively correlated) make it too cold. This is preferential
sampling in the design sense.

$q$ is unknown, so it is estimated from the simulated deployments. For launch-year cohort $c$ with $N_c$ floats per
replicate,

$$
\hat q^{(1)}_c(s)=\frac{\sum_{r}\sum_{i\in c,\,r}k_h(s-s_{ri})}{R\,N_c\int_{S}k_h(s-u)\,\nu(du)},
\qquad
\hat q=\sum_c N_c\,\hat q^{(1)}_c,
$$

where the sum runs over the cohort's profiles in the $R=1000$ replicates and $k_h$ is a Gaussian kernel with sd
$1/6^\circ$ in latitude and longitude and $2$ d in time, truncated at $4$ sd. The denominator is the kernel mass on
the ocean support $S$, which corrects for coasts and shelf. $\hat q^{(1)}_c$ is the intensity of one cohort-$c$
float, so a fold of $n_{k,c}$ cohort-$c$ floats has intensity $\hat q_k=\sum_c n_{k,c}\hat q^{(1)}_c$. When
$\hat q$ weights a replicate's own profiles, that replicate is left out ($R-1$ in the denominator). The plug-in
$\hat w=\hat q/\int\hat q\,d\mathbb P_y$ is what the maps below show.

## Mean field

Following @sukianto2026 (their eq. 5), which extends @ridgway2002 and @roemmich2009 with linear and quadratic time
trends, the mean field is a local polynomial regression in a fixed square window
$\mathcal W(x^*, y^*) = [x^* \pm \lambda] \times [y^* \pm \lambda]$, $\lambda = 5^\circ$, around each centre
$(x^*, y^*)$ of a $1^\circ$ grid. It uses all of the replicate's 2010--2019 profiles in the window:

$$
\begin{aligned}
m_{x^*, y^*}(x, y, t) = {}& \beta_0 + \beta_1 (x - x^*) + \beta_2 (y - y^*) + \beta_3 (x - x^*)(y - y^*)
+ \beta_4 (x - x^*)^2 + \beta_5 (y - y^*)^2 \\
&+ \sum_{k=1}^{6} \Bigl[\gamma_k \sin\tfrac{2\pi k \tau(t)}{365} + \delta_k \cos\tfrac{2\pi k \tau(t)}{365}\Bigr]
+ \nu_1 (t - t_D) + \nu_2 (t - t_D)^2,
\end{aligned}
$$

with $\tau(t)$ the yearday and $t_D$ = 2015-01-01. The coefficients are least squares over the window's profiles,
with a ridge of $10^{-8}\operatorname{tr}G$ on the Gram matrix $G$ for numerical stability. The window is never
widened: a centre with fewer than 60 profiles (three per coefficient) is left unfitted. The fit at the centre is

$$
\hat\mu(x^*, y^*, t) = \hat\beta_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{6} \Bigl[\hat\gamma_k \sin\tfrac{2\pi k \tau(t)}{365}
+ \hat\delta_k \cos\tfrac{2\pi k \tau(t)}{365}\Bigr] + \hat\nu_1 (t - t_D) + \hat\nu_2 (t - t_D)^2 .
$$

Off the grid, $\hat\mu(x, y, t)$ interpolates the four surrounding centres bilinearly, renormalized over the fitted
ones. This is our choice: @sukianto2026 define $\hat\mu$ only at the grid points. For DR, $\hat\mu_{-k}$ refits
every window without fold $k$'s floats. The refit is exact, by subtracting that fold's contribution to each
window's normal equations.

@fig-mean-series compares the mean field with the truth month by month.

::: {#cell-fig-mean-series .cell execution_count=6}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Top: monthly true box-mean OHC (solid) and the mean field (dashed; median over 200 replicates, band 5-95%). Bottom: mean-field error (dashed, with band) and map error (solid), medians over replicates (GJ per m2).](glorys_chain_files/figure-html/fig-mean-series-output-1.png){#fig-mean-series width=1199 height=704}
:::
:::


The mean field follows the seasonal cycle and the decade-long warming. What it leaves is interannual and
persistent: in box B the typical monthly error runs from $-1.7$ to $+0.7$ GJ m$^{-2}$, and in box A from $-0.7$ to
$+0.6$. Kriging the anomalies removes much of this, and the remainder is the map's bias.

## Kriging

The anomaly $Z - \hat\mu$ is modelled as a zero-mean Gaussian process with the locally stationary anisotropic
exponential covariance of @kuusela2018:

$$
k\bigl((x, y, t), (x', y', t')\bigr) = \phi \exp(-d) + \sigma^2 \mathbf 1\{\text{same point}\},
\qquad
d^2 = \Bigl(\tfrac{x - x'}{\theta_{\text{lon}}}\Bigr)^2 + \Bigl(\tfrac{y - y'}{\theta_{\text{lat}}}\Bigr)^2
+ \Bigl(\tfrac{t - t'}{\theta_t}\Bigr)^2,
$$

with $(\phi, \theta_{\text{lon}}, \theta_{\text{lat}}, \theta_t, \sigma^2/\phi)$ fixed per $2^\circ$ cell. The
parameters are fitted once, by windowed maximum likelihood with years as replicates and the median over months. The
fit uses GLORYS OHC minus the mean field from the real Argo positions, on the complete $1^\circ\times10$ d lattice of
2015--2019. They are therefore external to every replicate. They are also **oracle** values: no real analysis sees
the full field.

| | $\phi$ | $\theta_{\text{lon}}$ | $\theta_{\text{lat}}$ | $\theta_t$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Box A (median over cells) | 19.4 | 3.5° | 2.9° | 83 d |
| Box B (median over cells) | 48.9 | 2.4° | 1.5° | 38 d |

Prediction is simple kriging in continuous time. A target in cell $c$ conditions on all of the replicate's profiles
within $\pm 10^\circ$ and $\pm 180$ d and uses cell $c$'s parameters. The map is $\hat m = \hat\mu + \hat\eta$. The fold
map $\hat m_{-k} = \hat\mu_{-k} + \hat\eta_{-k}$ drops fold $k$'s floats from both stages. The kriging drop is exact,
by block downdates of the conditioning system.

## Cross-fit DR

The deployed floats are split into $K = 5$ folds by a random permutation within each launch-year cohort, so every
fold carries about a fifth of each cohort. For fold $k$, $I_k$ is the set of its floats' in-box profiles in year $y$,
with residuals $e_k(x_i) = Z_i - \hat m_{-k}(x_i)$ against the map fitted without them. Then

$$
\hat\theta_{\mathrm{DR}} = \frac1K\sum_{k=1}^K\Bigl\{Q_y(\hat m_{-k}) + \hat C_k\Bigr\},
\qquad
\hat C_k = \frac{\sum_{i\in I_k} v_i\,e_k(x_i)}{\sum_{i\in I_k} v_i},
\qquad
v_i = \frac{1}{\hat q_k(x_i)} .
$$

$\hat q_k$ is fold $k$'s intensity from above, computed without the evaluated replicate. This keeps the weights
independent of the floats they weight, which the unbiasedness argument (Campbell's theorem) requires.
$Q_y(\hat m_{-k})$ is fold $k$'s map estimate, and

$$
T_k=\theta_y-Q_y(\hat m_{-k})
$$

is what it misses: the error of the map fitted without fold $k$, with the sign of a correction. $\hat C_k$, a
$1/\hat q_k$-weighted (Hájek) mean of fold $k$'s residuals, estimates $T_k$. In practice $T_k$ is unknown because
$\theta_y$ is; here the truth is known, so $T_k$ can be computed and every correction checked against its target.
Subtracting $\theta_y$ from the estimator gives the exact identity

$$
\hat\theta_{\mathrm{DR}}-\theta_y=\frac1K\sum_{k=1}^K\bigl(\hat C_k-T_k\bigr),
$$

so DR's error is the average error of the five corrections, and DR is unbiased exactly when the corrections
are unbiased for their targets on average.

**Why five folds.** Cross-fitting needs only that each fold's map and weights be built without that fold's
floats; the identity above and the unbiasedness argument hold for any fixed $K\ge2$. $K=5$ is the usual choice in
cross-fitted estimation [@chernozhukov2018]. A larger $K$, up to leaving one float out, would bring each fold map
closer to the full map: a fold map here uses $80\%$ of the floats, and its bias in box A is $-0.12$ against $-0.10$
for the full map. It would not change what the correction does. The cost is computational: each fold needs its own
mean field and kriging map for every month, and leaving one float out would mean about $1000$ fold maps per
replicate instead of five. The residuals of one float are strongly correlated, so a fold must hold whole floats;
with five folds each box-year fold still has about $10$ floats in box A and $15$ in box B, enough for a stable
weighted mean. We have not run $K>5$.

# Where the floats sample: $\hat q$

@fig-intensity shows $\hat w$, the estimated intensity relative to its mean, next to the OHC field it samples.


::: {#cell-fig-intensity .cell execution_count=8}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![2017, box A (south) and box B (north). Left: annual-mean true OHC with one replicate's in-box profiles. Right: sampling intensity q-hat relative to its mean (log scale) with OHC contours (GJ per m2).](glorys_chain_files/figure-html/fig-intensity-output-1.png){#fig-intensity width=1209 height=594}
:::
:::


Floats are up to three times more dense than average in some places and under half as dense in others. In box B
the dense and sparse regions line up with the OHC gradient across the Gulf Stream.

::: {#cell-fig-intensity-grid .cell execution_count=9}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Quarterly-mean sampling intensity q-hat of the full deployment law relative to its annual mean over A u B (log scale, common colour scale), 2015-2019.](glorys_chain_files/figure-html/fig-intensity-grid-output-1.png){#fig-intensity-grid width=1046 height=1170}
:::
:::


@fig-intensity-grid shows $\hat q$ by quarter. The pattern is stable within and across years: box B is
sampled more densely than box A throughout (median $\hat w$ of $1.23$ vs $0.71$ over quarters), and the quarterly
5--95% range of $\hat w$ in box B ($0.79$--$1.88$) is only slightly wider than the annual one ($0.84$--$1.77$).

# Preferential sampling

The naive mean's expected bias is $\operatorname{Cov}_{\mathbb P_y}(w,Z)$ (Methods): how strongly the sampling
intensity lines up with OHC. @fig-naive compares the naive bias, averaged over 1000 replicates, with this
covariance computed from the kernel estimate $\hat w$ and the true field alone, without using any replicate's
naive mean.

::: {#cell-fig-naive .cell execution_count=10}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Naive bias (estimate minus truth, mean over 1000 replicates, +/- 2 Monte Carlo se) and the alignment Cov(w-hat, Z) of the kernel sampling intensity with OHC (GJ per m2).](glorys_chain_files/figure-html/fig-naive-output-1.png){#fig-naive width=758 height=429}
:::
:::


Floats under-sample warm water. The naive mean is 1.3--2.6 GJ m$^{-2}$ too cold in box B and A $\cup$ B, and the
covariance accounts for $94$--$98\%$ of it; the small remainder is smoothing in $\hat w$.

# The bias--variance trade-off

**Why DR adds variance.** By the identity in Methods, the map's error is $-T$ (its own miss) and DR's error is
$\frac1K\sum_k(\hat C_k-T_k)$. DR swaps the map's systematic miss for the sampling error of the corrections, and
three things make that error larger than the map's own variability:

* each $\hat C_k$ is a mean over one fold's profiles, about a fifth of the floats (about $10$ floats per box-year
  in box A and $15$ in box B), and the profiles of one float are strongly correlated, so it averages few
  independent pieces of information;
* the $1/\hat q_k$ weights are uneven, which lowers the effective sample size further (to about $80\%$ of the
  profile count in box A);
* each fold map is built from $80\%$ of the floats, so $Q_y(\hat m_{-k})$ is noisier than $Q_y(\hat m)$, and the
  average over five folds only partly recovers this.

**When DR lowers MSE.** Since $\text{MSE}=\text{bias}^2+\text{variance}$, DR beats the map exactly when the squared
bias it removes exceeds the variance it adds:

$$
\text{bias}^2_{\text{map}}-\text{bias}^2_{\text{DR}}\;>\;\operatorname{Var}_{\text{DR}}-\operatorname{Var}_{\text{map}}.
$$

Pooled over 2015--2019, box A removes $0.010$ (GJ m$^{-2}$)$^2$ of squared bias and adds $0.015$ of variance;
box B removes $0.0005$ and adds $0.054$. DR is therefore likely to win when the map's bias is persistent and large
next to the residual noise: when the target averages the variance away but not the bias (multi-year means, larger
regions), or when more floats per fold shrink the correction's variance.

# How DR reweights the kriging residuals

The map fitted without fold $k$ misses the truth by $T_k=\theta_y-Q_y(\hat m_{-k})$. DR estimates $T_k$ from the
fold-$k$ floats' residuals $e_k=Z-\hat m_{-k}$. Floats crowd where $q$ is large, so a plain average of the residuals is
tilted the same way as the naive mean. Weighting by $1/\hat q_k$ removes the tilt. @fig-dr-example shows one
replicate-year, picked for its large map error (box B 2017, replicate 171: map $+0.45$, DR $-0.02$ GJ m$^{-2}$).

::: {#cell-fig-dr-example .cell execution_count=14}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Replicate 171, box B, 2017. Left: error field of the map fitted without fold k. Middle: fold k's residuals at its floats' profiles, marker area proportional to the weight 1/q-hat. Right: per fold and averaged over folds, the target T_k, the plain residual mean and the weighted correction C_k (GJ per m2).](glorys_chain_files/figure-html/fig-dr-example-output-1.png){#fig-dr-example width=1187 height=468}
:::
:::


In the right panel each fold is one estimation problem. The black bar $T_k$ is what fold $k$'s map misses, the
target. The blue bar $\hat C_k$ is DR's estimate of it, and the grey bar is the same residuals averaged without
weights. A good correction has its blue bar close to the black one. Single folds are noisy (two of five here
correct in the wrong direction). What enters the estimator is the average over folds, the right-most group: DR's
error is the gap between the averaged blue and black bars, here $-0.53$ against $-0.51$.

@fig-corrections shows these fold averages for every replicate-year as errors. The first box is the error of the
fold maps alone, $-\bar T$. Adding the plain residual mean gives the second, and adding $\bar C$ gives the third,
which is DR's error exactly.

::: {#cell-fig-corrections .cell execution_count=15}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Per replicate-year (200 replicates x 5 years), errors after averaging over the five folds: the fold maps alone (-T-bar), the fold maps plus the plain residual mean, and the fold maps plus C-bar, which is the DR error (GJ per m2). Diamonds are means; bias and sd are printed above.](glorys_chain_files/figure-html/fig-corrections-output-1.png){#fig-corrections width=1309 height=450}
:::
:::


In box A the fold maps are $0.12$ GJ m$^{-2}$ too cold, and the plain residual mean removes only part of this
because it is tilted toward the crowded cells; the weighted correction leaves $-0.015$. In box B the fold maps are
nearly unbiased already ($-0.035$). The plain mean would push them to $-0.21$, the weighted correction leaves them at
$-0.04$, and the price is a larger spread (sd $0.35\to0.42$).

@fig-residual-cells shows where the weighted correction moves away from the plain mean. All held-out residuals are
pooled over the 200 replicates, five years and five folds and binned to $0.5^\circ$ cells. A profile's relative
weight is $r=\hat q_k^{-1}$ divided by its mean over the fold's profiles in that box-year, so
$C_k-\bar e_k=n_k^{-1}\sum_i (r_i-1)\,e_i$. The right panel is each cell's share of the average of this gap,
and over a box the shares sum to it exactly ($+0.03$ in box A and $+0.17$ in box B, GJ m$^{-2}$).

::: {#cell-fig-residual-cells .cell execution_count=16}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Held-out residuals pooled over 200 replicates, 2015-2019 and the five folds, per 0.5 deg cell with at least 30 residuals. Left: mean weight 1/q-hat_k relative to its fold mean (log scale). Middle: mean residual Z - m(-k) (GJ per m2). Right: the cell's contribution to the mean of C_k minus the plain residual mean.](glorys_chain_files/figure-html/fig-residual-cells-output-1.png){#fig-residual-cells width=1148 height=451}
:::
:::


In box B the densely sampled cells north of about $40^\circ$N (weight below $0.9$) have a mean residual of
$-0.54$ GJ m$^{-2}$: the map is too warm there, and these cells dominate the plain mean. Down-weighting them
provides $+0.09$ of the $+0.17$ shift, so most of the correction comes from shrinking the crowded cells, not from
boosting the sparse ones. In box A the residuals have nearly the same mean at every weight ($0.06$--$0.12$), so
reweighting changes little.

# Multi-year targets

The annual estimates of one replicate also give year-to-year changes and the five-year mean. Errors are close to
uncorrelated across years. So a change adds two years' variance while a persistent bias cancels, and the five-year
mean divides the variance by about five while the bias stays.

For changes the map wins everywhere. For the five-year mean DR wins in box A (MSE 0.009 against 0.017 (GJ m$^{-2}$)$^2$) and in
A $\cup$ B (0.011 against 0.014), because the map's bias no longer averages out against its variance. Box B still
favours the map.

# Kernel bandwidth

DR's remaining bias comes from smoothing in $\hat q$. Rebuilding $\hat q$ on a $3\times3$ grid of space and time
kernel widths, with the maps fixed, moves box B's DR bias steadily from $-0.10$ (widest) to $-0.02$ (narrowest).
Narrower kernels cost variance and leave places where $\hat q$ is nearly zero. Production uses $(1/6^\circ,2\text{ d})$,
the lowest box B MSE on the grid.

More simulated trajectories would let the kernel shrink. The smoothing bias of $\hat q$ falls as the kernel narrows,
roughly with its squared width, while the Monte Carlo noise of $\hat q$ grows as fewer simulated profiles fall
inside the kernel, roughly as $1/(R h_s^2 h_t)$ for $R$ replicates and widths $h_s,h_t$. With more replicates the
kernel can be narrowed at the same noise, so DR's remaining bias should go to zero as $R$ grows; this is standard
kernel asymptotics, not something tested here beyond $R=1000$. More trajectories do not reduce DR's variance over
deployments, which comes from the residuals of the one array actually deployed.

# Summary

* Floats preferentially sample cold water; the naive mean is biased by up to $-2.5$ GJ m$^{-2}$.
* The map is the most precise annual estimator, but keeps a persistent bias of $-0.1$ GJ m$^{-2}$ in box A.
* DR removes most of that bias at the price of more variance. It wins when the target averages variance away and
  leaves bias, such as the five-year mean in A and A $\cup$ B. It loses for single years and for changes.
* DR's remaining bias is kernel smoothing in $\hat q$, which narrower kernels or more replicates could reduce.
